# Initial OLS models for Residential & Commercial Properties in Lucas County

## Describing the Issue at Hand

-   The Lucas County Board of Revision (BOR) meets every fiscal year to review the values that were set on properties within the county by the Lucas County Auditor tri-annualy. The Auditor in the last evaluation (2021) used a third party company from Cincinnati to create a model that best describes that value of a property. While I was sitting on the BOR many complaints from professionals that work within the real estate industry, everyday taxpayers, and lawyers sparked a question that was bought up many times under different pretenses: ***"Does the model actually fit the data?"***. This and amongst other concerns were bought to question. Some other questions of interest are:

    -   ***Is square footage the best indication of the projected sale of a property?***

        -   The goal of solving this problem is to help professionals in lucas county to better assess residential properties so there is a fair market value of it.

        -   $H_{0}: \beta_{1} = \beta_{k} = 0$\$H\_{A}: \beta\*{1}\* \neq \beta{k} \neq 0 \$

    -   ***The year that a house was built isn't a deterministic causal variable.***

        -   Many of the BOR officers assumed that the year a property was built was causal on the sales price.

    -   ***I'm expecting majority of my variables to be correlated with each other - square footage determines how many bedrooms and baths can be put in a house. Also since the variables of interest in the data set do not change over time it makes since to initially use a standard OLS model. To be specific I will be using a log - level model so we can see how a one unit change in each variable affects the expected sale price of a parcel.***

        -   $$ ln(last sale price_{i}) = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}tla_{i} + \beta_{2}acres_{i} + \beta_{3}bedrooms_{i} + \beta_{4}baths_{i} + \beta_{5}yearbuilt_{i} + \epsilon $$

    ## Importing and Cleaning Data

    ```{r}
    library(tidyverse)
    library(readxl)

    Sales <- read_excel('/Users/deen/Documents/Education/Economic Research/Real Estate Prices/Copy of Data /Total Data Set.xlsx') |> 
      fill(acres) |> 
      fill(baths) |> 
      fill(bedrooms) |> 
      fill(yearbuilt) |> 
      fill(tla) |> 
      fill(`wall type`) |> 
      fill(zip)


    head(Sales)

    ```

I feel that maybe I need to rethink how I organize my data. I believe it would be easier to group my data by land use. This would allow me to focus on different property types (commercial, residential, etc).

```{r}

#We will try to different methods. The first one is by using the unique() function 
land_vector <- c(Sales$`land use`)
unique_land <- unique(Sales$`land use`)
sort(unique_land)
```

From the above we can now see what are the different types of land use and better assign each land use to a new data frame grouped by the hundreds. Something to be noted is that for parcels 400 - 499 these are all the taxable commercial real estate properties, 500 -599 are taxable residential properties with 510 - 513 being considered single residential homes, 520, 521 are duplexes, and 530, 531 are triplexes. 600 -699 are all tax exempt real property, while 700 - 799 are special tax abatement for improvements. I do not at this time know what are the 800s for. Lets start by seeing how many observations we can get for all the residential properties because these are the properties of interest.

### Transforming & Cleaning Residential Data

```{r}
install.packages("ggmap")
install.packages("tmaptools")
install.packages("sf")
install.packages("censusxy")
install.packages("rnaturalearth")
install.packages("rnaturalearthdata")
install.packages("tidygeocoder")
library(tidygeocoder)
library(sf)
library(tmaptools)
```

We need to combine some the address, city, state, and zip variables to one variable so we can get actual longitude and latitude:

```{r}
Sales_1 <- unite(Sales, col = "address", address, city, state, zip, sep = ",")
```

```{r}

geocode(Sales_1, address = address, method = "osm") 
```

So it turns out that there is a limit of 1 address per second using the previous method. We can try using Google's API but it does cost.

```{r}
library(ggmap)
```

```{r}
typeof(Sales_1$`land use`) #allows us to see what kind of data type the land use variable is 

resident_sales <- Sales_1 |> 
  filter(`land use` >= 500 & `land use` < 600)

print(resident_sales) 
```

Now we can check our new data frame to ensure that we are strictly dealing with residential properties:

```{r}
unique(resident_sales$`land use`) |> 
  sort()
```

```{r}
#Lets get an idea of what our individual data sets look like 

library(stargazer)

summary(resident_sales)


```

We have a lot of missing values for our variables and we should fill them with 0s or 1s or omit decide to them.

```{r}

#We can use the fill() function to fill the NA's using the next or previous values 

resident_data <- resident_sales |> 
  fill(`last sale price`) |> 
  fill(`appraised value`)
```

Now lets take a look at our summary of the variables again:

```{r}

summary(resident_data)
```

### Transforming & Cleaning Commercial Data

```{r}
commercial_sales <- Sales |> 
  filter(`land use` >= 400 & `land use` < 500)
commercial_sales
```

```{r}
summary(commercial_sales)
```

### Data Visualization

#### Residential Distributions

##### Last Sale Price Distribution

```{r}

ggplot(resident_data, aes(`last sale price`))+
  geom_histogram(bins = 50)
```

We can use a log() to transform this to get it to be a normal distribution:

```{r}
transformed_response <- log(resident_data$`last sale price`)
```

Now lets see a scatter plot of all the sales by tax district:

```{r}
ggplot(resident_data, aes(tla, `last sale price`))+
  geom_point(aes(colour = city))+
  geom_smooth()
```

##### Square Footage Distribution

```{r}
ggplot(resident_data, aes(tla))+
  geom_histogram(bins = 75)
```

##### Acres Distribution

```{r}
ggplot(resident_data, aes(acres))+
  geom_freqpoly()
```

##### Bedroom and Bath Bar Graphs

```{r}
ggplot(resident_data, aes(bedrooms))+
  geom_bar(color = "blue")
```

```{r}
ggplot(resident_data, aes(baths))+
  geom_bar(color = "green")
```

#### Commercial Distributions

```{r}
ggplot(commercial_sales, aes(`last sale price`))+
  geom_histogram(bins = 25)
```

For the population of both the commercial and residential properties - they follow an F distribution.

### OLS Models

```{r}
#Residential OLS Model 

res_regress1 <- lm(`last sale price` ~ tla + acres + bedrooms + baths + yearbuilt, data = resident_data)

stargazer(res_regress1, type = "text")
```

It seems that I have an issue with some values in my **y** variable, so we need to find where they are or if an NA exist within this value. It shouldn't sense we already transformed the data.

```{r}
x = resident_data$`last sale price`

if(is.null(x)) {
  fill(x)
} else {
  print("Data is clean of null values")
}

```

```{r}
typeof(resident_data$`last sale)
```
